newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court denies Reagan aide's libel appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court denies Reagan aide's libel appeal.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday let stand the dismissal of a libel lawsuit by a former White House National Security Adviser over a 1991 Esquire magazine article accusing him of being an Israeli spy.

The justices -- without any comment or dissent -- denied an appeal by Robert McFarlane, who served in the White House during Ronald Reagan's presidency in the 1980s, to reinstate his $30 million lawsuit.

A federal judge and then a U.S. Court of Appeals threw out the lawsuit because McFarlane had failed to show clear and convincing evidence Esquire published the article with "actual malice," as required in libel cases.

MacFarlane in his appeal asked the Supreme Court to revisit its historic 1964 libel ruling requiring that a public figure show a defendant acted with "actual malice -- knowledge the statements were false or reckless disregard for the truth.
Esquire replied that the justices should reject McFarlane's invitation "to turn back the clock" and upset more than three decades of American libel law.

The article by freelance author Craig Unger concerned the so-called "October Surprise" in which the 1980 Reagan-Bush campaign team allegedly tried to delay release of the American hostages in Iran until after the presidential election.

The lawsuit focused on a passage quoting Ari Ben-Menashe, a former Israeli spy. He alleged McFarlane had been "recruited" by Israeli spy Rafi Eitan and that McFarlane was the other American spy identified by investigators in the Jonathan Pollard Israeli spy case in the mid-1980s.
